pages.subtitle: Mars has no tectonic plates. So why does it shake?
paragraphs: On Earth, moving plates cause many quakes.
its crust acts like one giant plate, and it still trembles. Faults form as the planet slowly cools and shrinks. And sometimes a space rock falls from the sky.

secondarySection.title: Three questions nobody can answer yet

questions.question: Is Mars's core like Earth's?
questions.answer: Earth's outer core is liquid and its inner core is solid. NASA said scientists would keep checking InSight's data to see whether Mars is similar.

questions.question: How big is the core, really?
questions.answer: 1,830, then 1,780–1,810, then 1,650. The newest number isn't a final answer.

questions.question: Where are the missing quakes?
questions.answer: Cerberus Fossae speaks clearly. Tharsis stays silent. Shadow zones may hide some.

pages.closing: The mission ended. The questions remain.

pages.title: Inside the Machine That Listened to Mars
paragraphs: being sent to another planet. You can't walk around. You
anything yourself. You have one machine, and it must make its own power, place its
and send its discoveries home across space. That machine was
So how do you build a machine that listens to a planet?

pages.title: 1. The solar panels: the machine's lifeline
paragraphs: There are no power outlets on Mars. So InSight carried two circular solar panels, each about
across, that gave the lander its electricity.
At landing, the panels made about
of energy per Martian day. A watt-hour is a unit of energy, and 5,000 is enough to run an electric oven for
dust had cut that to about
engineers had the arm trickle sand beside a panel so the wind would knock dust loose, which added about
. It couldn't stop the decline, so the team switched instruments off one by one until the seismometer was the last one running.
A spacecraft needs a plan for its whole life, not only its first day.

promptBox.label: THINK LIKE AN ENGINEER:
promptBox.text: If you were designing InSight, how would you protect its power supply in a dusty place?

pages.title: 2. The lander body: built to stay put
paragraphs: was built on the proven design of NASA's
. The basic structure of its arm was first built for a Mars lander planned for
and later cancelled, then
. Its temperature and wind sensors were refurbished spares from
Unlike a rover, InSight never travelled. Studying the inside of
It needs a stable place to listen from.
Good engineering reuses what already works, then focuses on the one job that matters.

pages.title: 3. The robotic arm: the hands of the mission
paragraphs: Imagine working in a lab where you can only touch things through a robot arm, controlled from another planet. The arm was
long, with a
like a claw, at the end and a camera on the forearm.
It lifted
and the heat probe off the deck and set them on the ground. NASA lists
as the first mission to use a robotic arm to place instruments on the surface of another planet.
was meant for emergencies, such as helping the stuck mole. Before trying any move on Mars, the team practised on

paragraphs.text: ForeSight, a full-size twin at JPL

paragraphs: The most sensitive instruments worked best in direct contact with the ground.

promptBox.label: THINK LIKE AN ENGINEER:
promptBox.text: Why use an arm instead of attaching the instruments to the lander?

pages.title: 4. SEIS: the ears that listened to Mars
paragraphs: standing blindfolded in a room while someone knocks on the walls. Could the sounds tell you what's inside? That is the idea behind
it listens to waves travelling through a planet.
has two sets of sensors, one for slow, deep rumbles, sealed in a vacuum container, and one for quicker tremors. But wind and temperature swings add noise.
seismometers are often buried about
underground to keep their temperature steady.
couldn't build a vault on Mars, so engineers put
directly on the ground and covered it with the
built
with a skirt of chain mail and thermal blankets that settles over rocks.
Discovering what's hidden doesn't always mean seeing it. It means knowing how to read its signals.

promptBox.label: THINK LIKE A SCIENTIST:
promptBox.text: If waves travel differently through different materials, what could that tell us about the layers inside Mars?

pages.title: 5. HP³: the explorer that tried to dig deeper
paragraphs: built by
was a self-hammering spike that pulled a tether of temperature sensors behind it. Its target was about
down, to measure heat flowing out of Mars.
It needed friction from the soil to keep moving.
was clumpier than expected and didn't give it enough grip.
engineers tried new ideas, even pressing on the mole with the arm's scoop. The last session, about
made no visible progress. The heat-flow goal was not completed, but the effort taught scientists about the soil.
Engineering models are built on assumptions, and the real world doesn't always follow them.

promptBox.label: THINK LIKE AN ENGINEER:
promptBox.text: If you could redesign the mole, what would you change to help it grip unfamiliar soil?

pages.title: 6. RISE: measuring the invisible
paragraphs: needed no extra instrument on the ground. It used
. Scientists on Earth sent a signal through NASA's Deep Space Network, and the lander sent it back. Tiny changes in its frequency,
work like an ambulance siren changing pitch, and they reveal how Mars moves.
Those measurements showed how the planet wobbles because of

paragraphs.text: the sloshing of its liquid core

paragraphs: Not every instrument has to touch what it studies. Sometimes the information travels in the signals between two distant points.

pages.title: 7. TWINS and the weather station: the noise detectives
paragraphs: recording a whisper in a room full of people talking.
has the same problem: air pressure changes and wind create movements that can
So
carried a weather station.
supplied
measured wind and air temperature, a pressure sensor measured air pressure, and a magnetometer,
placed on the surface of another planet, measured magnetic changes. They collected data constantly so scientists could spot noise.
To understand a signal, you must understand the place where it was recorded.

pages.title: 8. The cameras: the eyes that connected Mars to Earth
paragraphs: One camera,
sat on the arm. The other,
sat on the lander below the deck, facing the work area. Both took
On landing day, a radio signal took
to reach Earth. So the team couldn't steer the arm like a video game. They planned each move, sent commands, then checked the returned images.
Remote robotics means making decisions with delayed information.

pages.title: 9. The long-distance link: from a dome on Mars to a file on your laptop
paragraphs: sent data
to orbiters circling Mars, which relayed it to NASA's Deep Space Network on Earth. Teams in

paragraphs.text: France and Switzerland, including the Marsquake Service led by ETH Zurich,

paragraphs: then reviewed it to detect, locate and classify every event. The data was archived for everyone to use. A team of only
ran the whole mission.

secondarySection.title: The machine was more than its parts
paragraphs: how its panels collected energy, how its arm placed delicate instruments, how SEIS listened, and how engineers used radio signals to investigate what they couldn't see.
wasn't successful because every part worked as planned. Some instruments achieved remarkable science. Others faced problems engineers couldn't overcome. Both outcomes taught us something.

paragraphs.text: Three problems it couldn't fully solve:

paragraphs: grip, dust, noise. What would you change? That's your next challenge.

pages.closing: The mission ended. The lessons remain.

It discovered what humans could not see.
But its legacy is still waiting.

engineering.title: Dust Accumulation on Solar Unit
engineering.disclaimer: Hypothetical future outpost engineering scenario (not historical InSight capability).
engineering.alertText: Solar efficiency decreasing. Martian dust accumulation detected.
engineering.prompt: Choose how to respond before regional winds intensify:

options.label: A. Activate cleaning mechanism
options.summary: Sweeps dust off panels; draws startup surge power and adds slight mechanical wear.
options.tradeoff: +12 Energy recovery · Minor actuator wear noted
options.outcome: Electromechanical wipers cleared most settled dust. Output recovered after a short startup power draw, though actuator wear increased slightly.
options.strength: Balanced recovery — effective when power reserves allow the cleaning surge.

options.label: B. Conserve power
options.summary: Throttles nonessential loads to protect battery reserves, slowing science.
options.outcome: Nonessential lab heaters and secondary relays entered low-power mode. Reserves stabilized cleanly, at the cost of paused science measurements.
options.strength: Low-risk preservation — avoids mechanical wear while keeping reserves steady.

options.label: C. Adjust panel orientation
options.summary: Tilts arrays toward afternoon sunlight; does not guarantee dust removal.
options.tradeoff: +6 Energy · Zero wear · Dust layer remains
options.outcome: Tracking actuators tilted the array to catch higher-angle sunlight without spending cleaning power, though settled dust still limits peak output.
options.strength: Zero-wear adjustment — modest gain without risking delicate moving parts.

event_1.title: Regional Martian Dust Storm
event_1.disclaimer: Simplified educational simulation of dust storm power trade-offs.
event_1.alertText: Suspended atmospheric dust is dimming incoming sunlight across Elysium Planitia.
event_1.prompt: Solar generation is falling. How will you manage the outpost grid?

options.label: A. Run active dust-clearing cycle
options.summary: Fights heavy dust buildup during the storm, costing energy and mechanical strain.
options.outcome: Active clearing kept the panels from choking completely, preserving science uptime at the expense of higher actuator strain.
options.strength: Keeps science running through low light, though repeated storm cycles stress hardware.

options.label: B. Switch to low-power standby
options.summary: Protects habitat and batteries by suspending active scientific sampling.
options.outcome: The outpost rode out peak dust opacity on low-power standby. Batteries stayed healthy, while science logging paused until skies cleared.
options.strength: Prioritizes crew & grid survival during severe sunlight drops.

options.label: C. Draw from stored battery reserves
options.summary: Maintains full habitat and science operations using stored reserves.
options.outcome: Battery banks bridged the storm gap so instruments kept recording dust-storm meteorology, leaving thinner energy margins for later cold.
options.strength: Maximizes storm science data, provided enough energy was saved earlier.

event_2.title: Severe Martian Cold Snap
event_2.disclaimer: Simplified thermal engineering simulation for a future crewed habitat.
event_2.alertText: Nighttime temperatures plunged sharply. Habitat hull heat loss is accelerating.
event_2.prompt: Protect habitat safety without exhausting outpost electrical reserves:

options.label: A. Increase active heating power
options.summary: Rapidly warms interior systems, drawing heavily on outpost electricity.
options.outcome: Auxiliary thermal loops stabilized cabin warmth quickly, pulling deeply from the solar battery bank.
options.strength: Fastest protection for habitat safety when energy reserves are healthy.

options.label: B. Deploy thermal insulation baffles
options.summary: Reduces heat loss passively with low power draw and balanced protection.
options.outcome: Deployable aerogel shields sealed thermal bridges around the airlock, cutting heat loss with minimal electrical penalty.
options.strength: Passive insulation reduces reliance on constant electrical heating.

options.label: C. Reduce nonessential science & redirect heat
options.summary: Reclaims waste heat and power for the habitat while pausing external experiments.
options.outcome: Science racks went into sleep mode and waste heat was routed into habitat walls, keeping both energy and safety steady.
options.strength: Smart load-shedding when energy is already tight.

event_3.title: Local Seismic Tremor Detected
event_3.disclaimer: Hypothetical engineering test scenario — real marsquakes vary in strength and do not typically damage surface structures.
event_3.alertText: Scientific Station recorded ground vibrations near the outpost foundation.
event_3.prompt: Respond to protect calibration and outpost stability:

options.label: A. Secure sensitive instruments
options.summary: Clamps delicate optics and levels sensors using slight stabilizer power.
options.outcome: Gimbal locks and leveling actuators protected the seismometer core, capturing clean aftershock data once tremors settled.
options.strength: Preserves high-value seismic science without shutting down the whole lab.

options.label: B. Reinforce vulnerable structures
options.summary: Engages outrigger anchors across the outpost to harden structural stability.
options.outcome: Foundation struts locked against the Martian regolith, boosting structural safety margins across the entire outpost.
options.strength: Strong structural resilience — especially valuable when combined with InSight soil lessons.

options.label: C. Temporarily pause scientific operations
options.summary: Parks instruments safely with minimal energy draw until ground motion stops.
options.outcome: Sensors safely retracted into park mode with near-zero power cost, avoiding drift at the cost of missing peak tremor readings.
options.strength: Conservative fail-safe that preserves electrical reserves.

moon.name: The Moon
moon.description: Humanity's primary stepping stone into the cosmos. NASA's Apollo missions left behind landing stages, rovers, and scientific packages that continue yielding discoveries.

equipment.name: Apollo 11 Lunar Module Descent Stage ("Eagle")
equipment.summary: The lower half and landing gear of the Eagle Lunar Module, used by Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin. Serves as the landing base and holds the commemorative stainless-steel plaque.
keyFacts: First crewed spacecraft landing base on another celestial body
Carries the commemorative plaque: "Here men from the planet Earth first set foot upon the Moon. We came in peace for all mankind."
Equipped with Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package (ALSEP) sub-assemblies

equipment.name: Lunar Laser Ranging Retroreflector (LRRR)
equipment.site: Tranquility Base & Fra Mauro & Hadley Rille
equipment.summary: Precision corner-cube prism arrays that bounce Earth-fired laser pulses back to terrestrial telescopes with picosecond time-of-flight resolution.
keyFacts: The only Apollo experiment that continues to collect scientific telemetry today
Measures the Earth-Moon distance down to a few millimeters
Proven that the Moon is slowly spiraling away from Earth at 3.8 cm per year

equipment.name: Lunar Roving Vehicle (LRV - "Moon Buggy")
equipment.summary: Electric four-wheel rover engineered by Boeing and Delco. Allowed astronauts to venture up to 35 kilometers away from the lunar module, carrying geologic drill cores and rock samples.
keyFacts: Capable of 13 km/h speed across jagged regolith slopes
Left permanently parked with high-gain directional antenna aimed at Earth
Apollo 17 rover drove a total record distance of 35.9 km across lunar valleys

equipment.name: Passive Seismic Experiment Package (PSEP)
equipment.summary: High-sensitivity long-period seismometers powered by radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs) to map the Moon's deep crustal stratification and core.
keyFacts: Detected over 12,000 seismic events, including deep tidal moonquakes and meteor impacts
Revealed that the Moon has a crust ~60 km thick and a small metallic core

mars.name: The Mars
mars.description: A rust-colored desert world shaped by ancient rivers, towering volcanoes, and violent dust storms. NASA robotic scouts have traversed hundreds of kilometers across Martian sands.

equipment.name: Perseverance Mars Rover
equipment.summary: NASA’s most sophisticated planetary explorer, seeking biosignatures of ancient microbial life in a dried river delta lakebed and caching core samples for future retrieval to Earth.
keyFacts: Carries MOXIE: First technology demonstration converting Martian CO₂ into breathable oxygen
Equipped with 23 advanced cameras, SuperCam Raman laser, and PIXL x-ray fluorescence
Cached over 25 pristine hermetic geological core samples for Mars Sample Return

equipment.name: Ingenuity Mars Helicopter ("Ginny")
equipment.summary: The historic first rotorcraft in human civilization to achieve controlled, powered flight on another planet, overcoming Mars’s ultra-thin atmosphere (less than 1% of Earth’s density).
keyFacts: Designed for 5 test flights; completed 72 flights spanning 17 kilometers
Dual counter-rotating carbon-fiber blades spinning at 2,400+ RPM
Served as an aerial scout finding traversable pathways for the Perseverance rover

equipment.name: Curiosity Rover (Mars Science Laboratory)
equipment.summary: The 1-ton rover that determined ancient Mars had freshwater lakes, neutral pH, and all chemical ingredients required to sustain microbial life billions of years ago.
keyFacts: Climbing Mount Sharp (Aeolis Mons), inspecting millions of years of layered Martian strata
Onboard Sample Analysis at Mars (SAM) laboratory detects organic carbon molecules
Has driven over 31 kilometers and beamed back hundreds of thousands of raw images

equipment.name: InSight Lander
equipment.summary: NASA's planetary crust observatory that listened to the heartbeat of Mars, placing the ultra-sensitive SEIS seismometer under a vacuum wind-shield dome.
keyFacts: Recorded over 1,319 marsquakes, revealing an active, tremor-filled interior
Measured Mars's liquid iron-nickel core with a radius of approximately 1,830 kilometers

equipment.name: Viking 1 & 2 Descent Landers
equipment.summary: Humanity's first successful long-duration surface stations on Mars, transmitting the first high-resolution color surface panoramas and atmospheric weather reports.
keyFacts: Operated for over 6 years on the Martian surface (Viking 1 ceased 1982)
Performed biological pyrolytic release and gas exchange soil experiments
